directAnswer: Pope Julius II was Giuliano della Rovere, nephew of Sixtus IV, who reigned from 1503 to 1513. Known as the warrior pope, he personally led campaigns to restore the Papal States, laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter's Basilica, founded the Swiss Guard, commissioned Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling and Raphael's Vatican rooms, and convened the Fifth Lateran Council.

sections.h2: Cardinal della Rovere and His Rivalry with the Borgias
paras: Giuliano della Rovere was born in 1443 at Albisola near Savona. When his uncle became Sixtus IV in 1471, Giuliano was made a cardinal and soon became one of the most powerful men in the Curia, helping to elect Innocent VIII.

He bitterly opposed Alexander VI and spent much of that pontificate in exile in France. After Pius III's brief reign, he won the conclave of 1 November 1503 in a matter of hours, reportedly having secured support through generous promises.

sections.h2: The Warrior Pope and the Italian Wars
paras: Julius II set out to recover papal territory lost or held by local lords and foreign powers. In 1506 he rode at the head of his troops to take Perugia and Bologna. He joined the League of Cambrai against Venice in 1508, then turned against France with the Holy League of 1511, determined to drive the French from Italy.

In January 1506 a contingent of Swiss soldiers arrived in Rome to serve as his guard, the origin of the Pontifical Swiss Guard that still protects the pope. Machiavelli discussed Julius in The Prince as a bold ruler whose impetuous style happened to suit his times.

On 18 April 1506 Julius laid the foundation stone of a new St. Peter's Basilica designed by Bramante, replacing the old Constantinian church. To fund the vast project he authorized indulgence preaching, a practice that would become a flashpoint under his successor.

He summoned Michelangelo, first to design his tomb and then to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling, completed in 1512. Raphael began the frescoes of the papal apartments now called the Raphael Rooms, including the School of Athens. Julius also displayed ancient sculptures such as the Laocoon, found in 1506, in the Belvedere courtyard, the seed of the Vatican Museums.

sections.h2: The Fifth Lateran Council and the Church in the Americas
paras: When French-backed cardinals summoned a rival council at Pisa in 1511 to challenge him, Julius responded by convening the Fifth Lateran Council, which opened in Rome in May 1512. He also issued a bull declaring simoniacal papal elections invalid.

In the New World he established the first dioceses in the Americas in 1511, on Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, and granted the Spanish crown broad rights of patronage over the Church there. Julius II died on 21 February 1513, leaving the papacy politically stronger and Rome transformed artistically.

keyFacts: Born Giuliano della Rovere at Albisola in 1443; nephew of Sixtus IV
Laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter's Basilica (18 April 1506)
Commissioned Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512)
Erected the first dioceses in the Americas (1511)

faqs.question: Why is Julius II called the warrior pope?
faqs.answer: He personally led papal armies, most famously in 1506 against Perugia and Bologna, and formed military alliances to recover the Papal States and expel the French from Italy.

faqs.question: Did Julius II found the Swiss Guard?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first Swiss guardsmen arrived in Rome in January 1506 at his request, and the corps has served the popes ever since.

faqs.question: What did Julius II commission from Michelangelo?
faqs.answer: His tomb, which includes the famous Moses now in San Pietro in Vincoli, and the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted between 1508 and 1512.
